newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Britain launches inquiry over budget leak.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Britain launches inquiry over budget leak.

text.p: Top secret documents revealing tax changes were leaked to a tabloid newspaper just hours before Britain's annual budget on Tuesday, causing acute embarrassment to the deeply unpopular Conservative government.

Prime Minister John Major's office vowed to "vigorously pursue" an inquiry into the source of the leak, the worst in 50 years. Other newspapers printed what they said were details of the last budget before an election due in the next six months.
The Daily Mirror, the paper which scored the scoop, held back from publication. But others said the budget included a cut in the basic tax rate to 23 percent from 24 percent.

Details reported in the Mirror's rival, the Sun, and in the London Evening Standard included a hike in cigarette taxes, a rise in petrol duty of five percent more than the rate of inflation and an increase in taxes on company cars.
The budget was also expected to cut corporation tax, which affects millions of firms, and raise the starting rate for inheritance tax, but to cut relief on profit-related pay.

Major's Downing Street office confirmed the bundle of documents handed in by the Mirror was genuine, but a Treasury spokesman said Clarke would not change the contents of the budget because of the revelations.
It said it had obtained an injunction from a judge to prevent details of the budget being published before Clarke reads his statement in parliament at around 1530 GMT.
A spokesman said that in the end the injunction was not used because it was overtaken by an agreement between the newspaper and the Treasury's lawyers not to publish.
But the Mirror put a different interpretation on events, saying it decided not to print details out of a sense of "public duty" and a desire not to cause chaos in financial markets.
London stocks, following a soaring New York market, hit new highs ahead of the budget. But generally financial markets, while intrigued by the leaks, did not react.
Sterling was unaffected and dealers took a sanguine view of what is more of a political than a financial embarrassment.
The budget is crucial to the government hopes of reversing the opposition Labour's opinion poll lead.

With an election no more than six months away, Clarke is expected to try to paint a rosy picture of Britain's economic future in a bid to convince voters they should stick with the Conservatives, in power since 1979.
But the leak, already being exploited by the opposition, is likely to cast a shadow over his carefully crafted statement.
Budget details are one of the most closely guarded secrets in British government circles. A previous finance minister had to resign in 1947 after leaking tax details to a journalist.

Labour's deputy campaign chief Brian Wilson said: "How can anyone trust Kenneth Clarke to run the economy when he loses half his Budget? This is just another reflection of the shambles which at present passes for Government."

Clarke has been heavily criticised because of his support for European moves towards a single currency, moves bitterly opposed by right wingers in the ruling party who want less and not more European integration.

These so-called Eurosceptics forced Clarke to face a parliamentary grilling on Monday, highly unusual on the eve of the budget, over his role in agreeing rules setting out the conditions for the creation of a single currency.
